top_cited_works.title: Origins and Structure of Spike-Type Rotating Stall
top_cited_works.abstract: In this paper, we describe the structures that produce a spike-type route to rotating stall and explain the physical mechanism for their formation. The descriptions and explanations are based on numerical simulations, complemented and corroborated by experiments. It is found that spikes are caused by a separation at the leading edge due to high incidence. The separation gives rise to shedding of vorticity from the leading edge and the consequent formation of vortices that span between the suction surface and the casing. As seen in the rotor frame of reference, near the casing the vortex convects toward the pressure surface of the adjacent blade. The approach of the vortex to the adjacent blade triggers a separation on that blade so the structure propagates. The above sequence of events constitutes a spike. The computed structure of the spike is shown to be consistent with rotor leading edge pressure measurements from the casing of several compressors: the centre of the vortex is responsible for a pressure drop and the partially blocked passages associated with leading edge separations produce a pressure rise. top_cited_works.title: A Criterion for Axial Compressor Hub-Corner Stall
top_cited_works.abstract: This paper presents a new criterion for estimating the onset of three-dimensional hub-corner stall in axial compressor rotors and shrouded stators. A simple first-of-a-kind description of hub-corner stall formation is developed which consists of (i) a stall indicator, which quantifies the extent of the separated region via the local blade loading and thus indicates whether hub-corner stall occurs, and (ii) a diffusion parameter, which defines the diffusion limit for unstalled operation. The stall indicator can be cast in terms of a Zweifel loading coefficient. The diffusion parameter is based on preliminary design flow variables and geometry. Computational simulations and single and multistage compressor data are used to show the applicability of the criterion over a range of blade design parameters. The criterion also enables determination of specific flow control actions to mitigate hub-corner stall. As an illustration, a flow control blade, designed using the ideas developed, is seen to produce a substantial reduction in the flow nonuniformity associated with hub-corner stall.

top_cited_works.title: An Investigation of Real Gas Effects in Supercritical CO2 Centrifugal Compressors
top_cited_works.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive assessment of real gas effects on the performance and matching of centrifugal compressors operating in supercritical CO2. The analytical framework combines first principles based modeling with targeted numerical simulations to characterize the internal flow behavior of supercritical fluids with implications for radial turbomachinery design and analysis. Trends in gas dynamic behavior, not observed for ideal fluids, are investigated using influence coefficients for compressible channel flow derived for real gas. The variation in the properties of CO2 and the expansion through the vapor-pressure curve due to local flow acceleration are identified as possible mechanisms for performance and operability issues observed near the critical point. The performance of a centrifugal compressor stage is assessed at different thermodynamic conditions relative to the critical point using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) calculations. The results indicate a reduction of 9% in the choke margin of the stage compared to its performance at ideal gas conditions due to variations in real gas properties. Mechanical Design, Manufacturing, and Rotordynamic Validation of a 1 MW Electrical Machine Demonstrator
recent_works.abstract: This paper presents the mechanical design, manufacturing processes, and rotordynamic validation of a fully air-cooled, 1 MW-class electrical machine intended for next-generation hybrid- and turbo-electric aircraft propulsion. The work builds upon the project overview described in the companion paper [1] entitled “Performance Assessment of a 1 MW Air-Cooled Electrical Machine Demonstrator for Turbo-Electric Propulsion.” Here, emphasis is placed on the mechanical design of the electrical machine: the high-speed permanent-magnet rotor, thin-lamination stator assembly, and the supporting bearing and damper architecture that enable stable supercritical operation at design speed. A comprehensive suite of risk-mitigation experiments—including spin-pit qualification, torque-transfer validation, stator winding process development, and rotordynamic response testing—was performed before full system integration. The assembled demonstrator achieved stable no-load operation at 12,500 RPM, confirming design predictions for radial growth, vibration amplitude, and critical-speed separation margin. recent_works.title: Power Electronics and Drive System Development for a 1 MW Air-Cooled Electrical Machine
recent_works.abstract: This paper describes the power-electronics (PE) and drive subsystem developed for the 1 MW fully air-cooled electrical-machine demonstrator presented in the companion paper [1] entitled “Performance Assessment of a 1 MW Air-Cooled Electrical Machine Demonstrator for Turbo-Electric Propulsion”. This presentation focuses on the experimental validation of the converter topology, packaging, and control hardware. The air-cooled distributed power converter predicts a specific power of 38 kW/kg (including cooling hardware, excluding structure). A master controller and multiplexer using an SPI interface, along with an absolute encoder for shaft-angle measurement, provided synchronization and control. The modular PE box with 10 inverter sets with DC bus rings and a multiplexer board successfully operated during no-load tests up to rated speed of 12,500 RPM. Currents were circulated to 80 ARMS per inverter at low speed, generating rated torque per inverter. In coupled operation, synchronized control across multiple inverter modules was achieved, with stable regulation of current, torque, and speed. recent_works.title: Performance Assessment of a 1 MW Air-Cooled Electrical Machine Demonstrator for Turbo-Electric Propulsion
Thermal Performance Assessment of an All-Air-Cooled 1 MW Electric Machine for Turboelectric Propulsion
recent_works.abstract: This paper presents the design, modeling, and experimental validation of the all-air thermal management system developed for a 1 MW-class electrical machine demonstrator intended for hybrid- and turbo-electric propulsion. The work builds upon the system described in the companion paper [1] entitled “Performance Assessment of a 1 MW Air-Cooled Electrical Machine Demonstrator for Turbo-Electric Propulsion” and focuses on the architecture, modeling, and structural integration of the cooling system. The demonstrator eliminates liquid coolants entirely, relying on suction-driven airflow through the airgap and additively manufactured heat exchanger (HEX) integrated in the aft frame. Computational and experimental efforts guided geometry optimization of the HEX around Reynolds numbers near 8,000. Testing confirmed that the air-cooling system maintained hot spot winding temperatures below 58.5°C at full speed under no-load conditions, achieving at least a 46.5°C reduction compared with uncooled operation.
